paragraphs: Tzarik kol adam lehizzaher libtzoa happat shemmebarek alayv hammotzi bemaqom shenneepa yapeh sheshshalat bo haesh yoter, veraq zaqen shei epshar lo leekol bemaqom shenneepa yapeh mechamat shehu qasheh az yibtza mimmaqom harak:

clarification.explanation: Every person must be careful to cut the bread over which he recites the blessing of HaMotzi specifically at the place where the bread was baked well, since the fire had more effect there. But an elderly person for whom it is difficult to eat from the harder place (that baked well) should cut from the soft place.
takeaways: The HaMotzi slice should be cut from the place that baked best.
An elderly person for whom hard bread is difficult should cut from the soft place.

paragraphs: Ameru rabbotenu za"l (berakot nb, b) tekep lintilat yadayim seuda, veal ken asur lehitasseq ben netila lehammotzi beezeh eseq, denimtza beisqo bo hare zeh massicha dato mehasseuda, vaapillu eseq kol dehu im tzarik ledaqdeq bo nimtza hu massicha dato dehaynu apillu lirot matbea im hu tob o ra, o lirot hammoreh shaot ladaat kamma hashshaa vekayyotze bazeh ki meachar detzarik ledaqdeq hare zeh massicha dato misseuda ben netilat yadayim useuda veasur, veken yizzaher shello yedabber ben netila lebirkat hammotzi, velo od ella apillu bishtiqa lo yapsiq, ella tekep bigmar hanniggub yebarek hammotzi veyibtza, ubediabad muttar, vetzarik lehazhir lekattechilla shello yishheh ben niggub lehammotzi kede hilluk k"b amma, vetzarik zerizut rab kede lehizzaher bekak:

clarification.explanation: Our Sages said: immediately following the washing of the hands comes the meal. Therefore it is forbidden to engage in any activity, even a minor one, between washing the hands and reciting HaMotzi — because any activity requiring concentration (for example, checking whether a coin is good, or looking at a clock) distracts one's mind from the meal that is supposed to follow immediately. Likewise, one should not speak between the washing and the blessing of HaMotzi, and should not even pause in silence — rather, immediately upon finishing drying the hands one should recite HaMotzi and cut the bread. After the fact, if time has passed, it is permitted. Ideally, one should be careful not to delay between drying and HaMotzi more than the time it takes to walk twenty-two amot, and this requires great alacrity to observe.
takeaways: It is forbidden to engage in anything requiring concentration (checking a coin, a clock, etc.) between washing the hands and HaMotzi.
One should not speak between the washing and HaMotzi — the blessing should be recited immediately upon finishing the drying.
Ideally, one should not delay more than the time of walking 22 amot between the drying and HaMotzi.

paragraphs: Halika mibbayit lebayit, apillu hilluk meat asur, vetzarik lehazhir hamon haam bazeh ki lipamim qopetzim lehabi mitpachat o melach vekayyotze mecheder lecheder ubediabad shari:

clarification.explanation: Walking from room to room, even a short walk, is forbidden between washing the hands and HaMotzi — and the public must be cautioned about this, because people sometimes jump up to bring a napkin, salt, or the like from another room. After the fact, if one has already walked, it is permitted.
takeaways: It is forbidden to walk from room to room (even for a minor need like bringing salt) between the washing and HaMotzi; after the fact it is permitted.

paragraphs: Katub beseper keter malkut ketibat yad: qodem kol seuda yomar "mizmor ledavid Adonai roi veku'", shebbo z"n tebot, shello yechsar mezono umazon hannepesh, gam yomar baqqashat yehe raava min qodem attiqa qaddisha veku', veyomar pasuq (shir hashshirim h, ) "bati ligne veku'" ad "iklu reim shetu veshikru dodim" ad kan. venireh vadday dekol zeh yomar qodem netilat yadayim, vegam nosach "leshem yichud qudesha berik hu ushekinatah", sheqqodem haakila vehabbaqqasha gam ken yomar qodem netila, ak haolam nohagim lomar mizmor Adonai roi ben netila lebirkat hammotzi, veap al pi sheyyesh mepaqpeqim bazeh mishshum hepseq en limchot beyadam:

clarification.explanation: It is customary to recite several formulas before the meal: the Psalm "A Psalm of David: the Lord is my shepherd" (which contains fifty-seven words, corresponding to the numerical value of "zan" — a name indicating that God sustains and provides, hinting that one's sustenance and the sustenance of his soul will not be lacking), a special request ("May it be the will before the Holy Ancient One"), and a verse from Song of Songs ("I have come into my garden... eat, friends, drink, and be inebriated, loved ones"). All these, as well as the formula "For the sake of the unification of the Holy One, blessed be He, and His Shechinah," are properly said before the washing of the hands. Nevertheless, the prevailing custom is to say "A Psalm of David: the Lord is my shepherd" between the washing and the blessing of HaMotzi, and although there are those who question this out of concern for an interruption, one should not protest against those who follow this custom.
takeaways: Preparatory formulas for the meal (the Psalm of David, requests, verses from Song of Songs) are preferably said before washing the hands.
The Psalm "The Lord is my shepherd" has fifty-seven words, corresponding to "zan" — a hint that God provides sustenance and nothing will be lacking for body or soul.
The prevailing custom is to say "The Lord is my shepherd" between the washing and HaMotzi — one should not protest against it despite the reservations raised.

paragraphs: Yitten shette yadayv al happat bishat beraka sheyyesh bam asar etzbaot keneged asar mitzot hatteluyot bappat, veellu hem lo tacharosh beshor vachamor, vesadeka lo tizra kilayim, veleqet veshikcha upea, ubikkurim, uteruma, umaaser rishon, umaaser sheni, o masar ani, vechalla, vegam keneged eser melakot sheyyesh min hacharisha ad haapiyya ki bekol melaka naasa berur nitzotze qedushsha kannoda, lekak yesh asara tebot bebirkat hammotzi, vaasara tebot bappasuq enay kol veku' (tehillim qmh, tv):

clarification.explanation: At the time of the blessing of HaMotzi, one should place both hands on the bread, so that the ten fingers allude to the ten commandments that depend on bread: the prohibition of plowing with an ox and a donkey together, the prohibition of sowing a field with mixed species, gleanings, forgotten sheaves, and the corner of the field, first fruits, terumah, first tithe, second tithe (or the tithe for the poor), and challah. They also allude to the ten labors performed from plowing until baking, in each of which sparks of holiness are clarified. Therefore there are ten words in the blessing of HaMotzi, and also ten words in the verse "The eyes of all look to You expectantly."
takeaways: One places both hands (ten fingers) on the bread during HaMotzi, alluding to the ten commandments dependent on bread and the ten labors of its production.

paragraphs: Tzarik ledaqdeq ulehadgish behe" shel hammotzi keillu yesh betok meloah he" acheret, laken yaarik bah meat veyagbihenna beqol keillu mazkirah bipne atzmah kazeh "h-motzi" kede sheyyukal lekavven bimloah he" acheret vekannizkar beshaar hammitzot lerabbenu za"l, ukesheyyaggia letebat hammotzi bihyoto maarik behe" az yitten et happat zaqup ben shette yado veyagbihennu qetzat, veyizzaher latet rivvach ben tebat lechem uben tebat min haaretz, ubesiddur rabbenu harasha"sh za"l katub: tannicha shette yadeka al happat, utekavven lehashpia mikkol haeser sepirot al hammalkut hanniqret lechem, vetadgish hah' dehammotzi, ubemillat hammotzi tagbihha shette yadeka vehallechem baemtza ad kan leshono, veim yesh lo bet yad (kepapot) tzarik lahasiro bebirkat hammotzi detzarik shettihyena yadayv mammash al happat:

clarification.explanation: One should emphasize and slightly lengthen the letter heh in the word "HaMotzi," as though there were another hidden heh within its spelled-out form, and raise the voice slightly on it — in order to have intention for the spelling of that letter. When reaching the word "HaMotzi" while lengthening the heh, one should hold the bread upright between the two hands and raise it slightly, and leave a slight gap between the words "lechem" (bread) and "min ha'aretz" (from the earth). In the Rashash's prayer book it is written: place both hands on the bread, intend to draw down the flow of the ten sefirot to the Malchut (called "bread"), emphasize the heh of "HaMotzi," and at the utterance of the word "HaMotzi" raise both hands with the bread in between. One who wears gloves must remove them for the blessing of HaMotzi, because the hands must actually touch the bread.
takeaways: Emphasize and lengthen the heh in "HaMotzi," and raise the bread slightly while saying it.
Remove gloves for the blessing of HaMotzi — the hands must touch the bread directly.

paragraphs: Lo yibtza mimmaqom shennitchabbera battannur im chabertah demecheze kechaser, gam lo yibtza bimqom sedeq vaapillu shenneepa oto maqom yapeh yoter, ubaal habbayit hu atzmo botzea "p sheyyesh oreach gadol mimmennu, umihu yakol lachaloq kabod laoreach sheyyebarek hu birkat hammotzi veken nohagim:

clarification.explanation: One should not cut from the place where two parts of the bread joined together in the oven, because it looks as though something is missing there (a blemish in the bread's appearance at that spot); nor should one cut at a place with a crack, even if the bread baked better there. The master of the house himself is the one who cuts the bread, even if a guest greater than him in stature is present — but he may extend the honor to the guest of reciting the blessing of HaMotzi, and this is indeed the custom.
takeaways: Do not cut from the joining point of two bread pieces in the oven, nor from a cracked spot.
The master of the house cuts the bread himself, but may honor a distinguished guest with reciting HaMotzi.

paragraphs: Lo yibtza perusa qetanna pachot mikkazzayit shennireh ketzar ayin, velo yoter mikkabbetza shennireh keraabtan, bammeh debarim amurim bechol veokel lebaddo, abal beshabbat apillu okel lebaddo shari libtzoa gedola likbod shabbat, veken bechol im okel im bene beto muttar libtzoa gedola kede litten min happerusa hazzot shebbotzea lekol echad veechad kazzayit, veen hammesubbin rashshain litom ad sheyyitom habbotzea, lepikak habbotzea yitom techilla vech"k yechalleq lamsubbin:

clarification.explanation: One should not cut a slice smaller than a kezayit, since that appears stingy, nor larger than a kebeitzah, since that appears gluttonous — this is specifically on a weekday, when a person eats alone. But on Shabbat, even when eating alone, it is permitted to cut a large slice in honor of Shabbat; and likewise on a weekday, when eating with the members of his household, it is permitted to cut a large slice in order to distribute a kezayit to each of those seated. Those seated may not taste until the one who cut tastes first — therefore the one who cut should taste first, and only afterward distribute to those seated.
takeaways: The HaMotzi slice should be between a kezayit and a kebeitzah on a weekday for one eating alone; on Shabbat, or when eating with others, a large slice is permitted.
Those seated do not taste before the one who cut — he tastes first and then distributes.

paragraphs: Habbotzea lehotzi hamsubbin yede chobatam yebarek beqol ram benachat kede sheyyishmeu hamsubbin et habberaka kullah bilti chesron teba achat, veyizzaher sheyyekavven lehotziam yede chobatam vegam hem yitkavvenu latzet yede chobatam bebirkato, veyesh chasidim medaqdeqin bekol beraka asher yebareku lehotzi bah acherim yede chobatam sheyyomru bepihem beperush qodem habberaka "hareni mekavven lehotzi yede choba kol hashshomea qoli bibraka zo", vehu minhag yapeh ki yizdammen shehaadam libbo tarud veeno mekavven veim yargil bekak bevadday yekavven, gam hamsubbin yihyu nizharim laanot amen beqol ram sheggam hambarek yekavven leammen sheomerim veyotze yede chobat amen, veoreach sheraa baal habbayit mebarek beraka chatupa uqetupa, o shechoshesh sheeno mekavven alayv az yebarek haoreach leatzmo belachash al happerusa behetznea kede shello yargish baal habbayit mippene darke hashshalom, veken hainyan beben hassomek al shulchan abiv sheyyaaseh kak im nitzrak lekak:

clarification.explanation: One who cuts the bread in order to discharge those seated of their obligation should recite the blessing aloud and calmly, so that everyone hears all the words of the blessing without any omission. He should intend to discharge their obligation, and they must intend to be discharged by his blessing. There are pious people who make a practice, with every blessing they recite in order to discharge others, of stating explicitly before the blessing: "I hereby intend to discharge the obligation of all who hear my voice in this blessing" — a fine custom, because sometimes the one reciting the blessing's mind is preoccupied and he lacks intention, and such an explicit statement helps him. Those seated must also be careful to answer Amen aloud, so that the one reciting the blessing may also intend regarding the Amen they say and thereby fulfill his own obligation of Amen. A guest who sees the master of the house reciting a hurried, clipped blessing, or suspects he is not having intention for him, should recite the blessing quietly for himself over his own slice, discreetly, so that the master of the house does not notice, for the sake of peaceful relations — and a son who relies on his father's table should act likewise in a similar situation.
takeaways: One who cuts to discharge others recites the blessing aloud, and it is proper to state explicitly that he intends to discharge everyone.
Those seated answer Amen aloud.
A guest who suspects the master of the house lacks intention for him should recite the blessing quietly for himself, without offending the master of the house.

paragraphs: Mitzva lehabi melach veyatbil happat shelosh peamim bammelach ki ken tzarik "p hassod, vikavven shehallechem hu mispar shelosh peamim hvy"h shehem shelosha chasadim, vehem mimmatteqim shelosha geburot haremuzim bemelach shehem gam ken mispar shelosh peamim hvy"h keminyan melach, veim berak hammotzi velo hebiu hammelach lo yamtin ella yibtza miyyad veyokal ubeet sheyyabiu hammelach al hashshulchan ad achar birkat hammazon dehashshulchan domeh lammizbeach uketib (vayyiqra b, yg): "al kol qarebbaneka taqrib melach", vegam hu mesuggal lehagen min happuraniyyot veyesh nohagin lehannicha al hashshulchan keli sheyyesh bo ezob veken katub beshem rabbenu haari"y za"l, uminhag yapeh venakon hu dehaezob hu besod hayyesod hahanqara tzaddiq siman laddabar vetzaddiq al shulchan yabo, veayyen bazzohar haqqadosh haazinu dap rtz"t ubebeur sham beinyan haezob yeuyyan sham:

clarification.explanation: It is a mitzvah to bring salt and dip the bread in it three times, as is proper according to the Kabbalah: the bread corresponds to three times the name Havayah (the three attributes of Chesed), which sweeten three attributes of Gevurah alluded to in the salt (which is likewise equal in gematria to three times Havayah, the numerical value of the word "melach"). If one has already recited HaMotzi and the salt has not yet been brought, one should not wait — one should cut and eat immediately, and the salt may be brought to the table at any point up until after Grace after Meals, since the table resembles the altar (as it is said, "With all your offerings you shall offer salt"), and salt is also efficacious to protect against misfortune. Some are accustomed to place a vessel with hyssop on the table, as mentioned in the name of the Ari, of blessed memory — a fine custom, since the hyssop is a mystical symbol of the Yesod, called "Tzaddik," alluding to the verse "and the righteous one shall come to the table."
takeaways: It is a mitzvah to dip the bread in salt three times, based on the mystical significance of three times Havayah in both the bread and the salt.
If the salt was not brought by the time of HaMotzi, one should not wait — one cuts and eats immediately, and the salt may arrive later.
There is a fine custom of placing a vessel with hyssop on the table, based on the Kabbalah.

paragraphs: Yizzaher shello yizroq happerusa lipne hamsubbin ella yannicha lipnehem ad maqom sheyyado maggaat, velo yitten happerusa beyad hamsubbin deen notenim bayyad ella leabel bar minnan, veal ken yizzaher bazeh gam bebanim haqqetannim shello yitten happerusa beyadam ella yannicha lipnehem vehem notelim:

clarification.explanation: One should not throw the slice to those seated, but rather place it before them within reach of their hand, and should not hand it directly into their hand — because handing something directly into the hand is a practice of mourning. One should be careful about this even with young children — placing the slice before them rather than handing it directly into their hand.
takeaways: Do not throw the bread slice to those seated — place it within their reach, not directly into their hand (this is a mourning practice).

paragraphs: Lo yitten libhema chayya veop apillu hattehorim min hallechem shebberak alayv hammotzi, velitmeim lo yitten lechem veshum maakol min habba al hashshulchan kelal, veken yizzaher shello yitten leakku"m maakol min hashshulchan vaapillu yishmeeli sheeno obed aboda zara, veraq im yesh chashash eba let lan bah, mippene shehashshulchan omed dugmat hammizbeach deshulchano shel adam mekapper alayv (menachot tzz.) lekak yizzaher bazeh:

clarification.explanation: One should not give to a domesticated animal, a wild animal, or a fowl — even kosher ones — from the bread over which HaMotzi was recited. To non-kosher animals one should not give any food from the table at all. Likewise, one should not give food from the table to a non-Jew, even an Ishmaelite who does not worship idols — except where there is concern of enmity (hostile relations), in which case it is permitted. The reason: the table resembles the altar, and "a person's table atones for him," so one must be careful regarding its sanctity.
takeaways: Do not give from the bread over which the blessing was recited to animals (even kosher ones) or to a non-Jew, since the table resembles the altar and atones for the person.
It is permitted to give to a non-Jew only where there is concern of enmity (hostile relations).

paragraphs: En rashshay habbotzea libtzoa ella ad sheyyikleh amen merob hamsubbin, veachar habberaka vehabbetzia yokal miyyad velo yasicha ben beraka laakila vaapillu amen deqaddish lo yaaneh ad sheyyitom ubeshum open lo yasicha ben beraka laakila, veim sach bidbarim chitzonim tzarik lachazor ulebarek, veim sach bidbarim hashshayyakim lasseuda "p dela shayeki libraka kegon sheamar habiu melach vekayyotze en tzarik lachazor ulebarek ulekattechilla yizzaher apillu bidbarim hashshayyakim libraka shello yasicha ad sheyyokal:

clarification.explanation: The one who cuts the bread is permitted to cut only after the majority of those seated have finished answering Amen to his blessing. After the blessing and cutting, he must eat immediately and not speak between the blessing and the eating — and he should not even answer Amen to Kaddish before he has tasted. Under no circumstances should he converse between the blessing and the eating. If he spoke of extraneous matters (unrelated to the meal), he must go back and recite HaMotzi anew. But if he spoke of matters relevant to the meal (such as "bring salt"), even though unrelated to the blessing itself, he need not recite the blessing again. Nevertheless, ideally he should be careful not to speak at all, even about matters relevant to the meal, until he has eaten.
takeaways: The one who cuts eats immediately after the blessing without speaking at all, not even answering Amen to Kaddish, until he tastes.

Speaking of extraneous matters between the blessing and the eating requires reciting the blessing again; speaking of matters relevant to the meal itself does not require this, but ideally should still be avoided.

paragraphs: Apillu shehiknis hammaakol lepiv veloaso kol od shello bala lo yasicha, umikkol maqom im sach qodem shebbala apillu bidbarim chitzonim en tzarik lachazor ulebarek, ulekattechilla nakon lehizzaher shello yasicha kelal ad sheyyigmor leekol kazzayit mipperusat hammotzi:

clarification.explanation: Even after placing food in his mouth and chewing it, as long as he has not yet swallowed, he should not speak. Nevertheless, if he spoke before swallowing, even of extraneous matters, he need not go back and recite the blessing again. Ideally, it is proper to be careful not to speak at all until finishing the eating of a kezayit from the HaMotzi slice.
takeaways: One should not speak even while chewing before swallowing; if one did speak before swallowing, there is no need to recite the blessing again, but ideally one should avoid speaking until finishing a kezayit.

paragraphs: Im amar tenu maakol libhema hare zeh chashub debarim hashshayyakim lasseuda, mippene deasur leadam leekol qodem sheyyitten maakol libhemto, veim amar tenu mayim libhema yesh lehistappeq vekannizkar bechesed lealpayim siman qs"z ot y' veayyen baacharonim al ken bikhay gavna tob sheyyeharher habberaka belibbo:

clarification.explanation: If he said "give food to the animal" — this is considered a matter relevant to the meal (and not a distraction), since a person is forbidden to eat before giving food to his animal. But if he said "give water to the animal" — there is room for doubt whether this is so (Chesed LeAlafim, and see the later authorities); therefore in such a case it is best that he merely contemplate the blessing in his heart.
takeaways: "Give food to the animal" is a matter relevant to the meal and not a distraction, since one is forbidden to eat before feeding one's animal.
"Give water to the animal" is doubtful; therefore it is best to contemplate the blessing in one's heart.

paragraphs: Im sach habbotzea bidbarim chitzonim sheddino lachazor ulebarek vehamsubbin lo hipsiqu yatzeu yede chobatam, veokelim, veen tzerikim lekavven libraka sheniyya shel habbotzea, veim sachu hamsubbin leachar shettaam habbotzea qodem sheyyitamu hem yesh pelugta bazeh vesapeq berakot lehaqel, velaken yeharharu habberaka bilbabam veyoklu:

clarification.explanation: If the one who cut spoke of extraneous matters requiring him to go back and recite the blessing again, but those seated themselves did not interrupt (did not speak), they have already discharged their obligation through the first blessing and may eat, and need not intend to be discharged by the second blessing of the one who cut. But if those seated themselves spoke after the one who cut had tasted and before they themselves had tasted, there is a dispute about the law in this case — therefore, since it is a doubt regarding blessings, to be resolved leniently, they should contemplate the blessing in their hearts and eat.
takeaways: An extraneous interruption by the one who cut (requiring him to repeat the blessing) does not affect those seated if they themselves did not speak — they have already discharged their obligation.
If those seated spoke before tasting themselves, there is a doubt, resolved by contemplating the blessing in one's heart.

paragraphs: Yesh nohagim leekol sheyare perusat hammotzi besop hasseuda mishshum chibbub mitzva ukede sheyyishshaer taam hammotzi bepiv uketib baruk tanaka umisharteka veyesh bazeh tiqqun lipgam habberit uminhag yapeh hu, ak bitnay deqim leh benapsheh shello yishkachenna deim shakach velo akalah may ahane leh veadderabba migraot natan veayyen bekap hachayyim siman k"g ot y"g, lekak hashshakchan lo yinhog bekak. veal kol panim yizzaher haadam leekol chatikat pat meat min hashshulchan samuk mammash lintilat mayim acharonim:

clarification.explanation: Some are accustomed to eat the remainder of the HaMotzi slice at the end of the meal, out of love for the mitzvah and so that the taste of the HaMotzi blessing remains in the mouth — alluding to the verse "Blessed shall be your basket and your kneading-trough" — and there is in this also a rectification for the blemish of the covenant. It is a fine custom, but on condition that the person is confident he will not forget to eat the remainder — for if he forgot and did not eat it, he gained nothing, and indeed caused himself a deficiency. Therefore, one who is forgetful should not follow this practice. In any event, a person should be careful to eat a small piece of bread from the table right before the washing of the final waters (mayim acharonim).
takeaways: It is a fine custom to save a piece of bread from HaMotzi and eat it at the end of the meal — but only for one confident he will not forget (otherwise it is better to forgo it).
In any case, one should eat a bit of bread from the table right before washing the final waters.
